requirements.name: single ownership split between session state, page ui state, operation state, and selectors
key UX: Server-synced chat truth stays in the session domain, including workspace, thread, active turn, turn status, waiting signals, messages, notices, pending requests, runtime preferences, runtime options, and stream metadata.
Only page-level UI concerns that affect cross-surface interaction rules are centralized in chat-page state, such as the active primary overlay and other shared gating inputs.

Async action progress stays in a dedicated operation state layer instead of being scattered across unrelated hooks, so the page can consistently express sending, interrupting, restarting, loading thread history, workspace switching, request submission, and workspace file actions.
All user-facing enable and disable behavior is computed through selectors and view-model rules rather than being recomputed ad hoc inside multiple components.

requirements.name: unified page interaction states without introducing new ui
key UX: The page behavior is driven by a small set of unified interaction states such as bootstrapping, ready-idle, awaiting-requests, running, restarting, auth-required, and load-error, even if the visible UI stays the same as today.
The page does not add new persistent notice regions, modals, or error widgets during this refactor; the existing UI keeps its current presentation while consuming clearer state semantics underneath.

Selectors expose stable behavior like canSend, canInterrupt, canSwitchWorkspace, canRestart, canOpenExplorer, and canSubmitPendingRequests so current components can keep rendering without new visual redesign.

requirements.name: sending behavior is gated by one unified readiness rule
key UX: The composer may send only when the session is ready, a workspace is present, there are no unresolved pending requests, the page is not restarting, the current interaction state allows fresh input, and the draft contains non-whitespace text.
Client-side send-in-flight state and server waiting-for-input state are unified behind selectors so the UI no longer combines separate booleans in page code to decide whether input is enabled.
A successful send clears the draft and transitions the page into the running state, while a failed send keeps the draft content intact and surfaces the error through the existing shared error outlet.

requirements.name: running turn behavior supports interrupt and forced restart
key UX: When a turn is actively running, the page stays in a running interaction state that blocks normal fresh-message sending and workspace switching while still allowing transcript browsing and other explicitly allowed side actions.
Stop or interrupt is available only while a turn is actively running and no interrupt action is already pending.

Restart remains allowed even during a running turn and acts as a higher-priority forced operation; once restart begins, the page enters the restarting state and normal chat interactions are blocked until recovery.

requirements.name: pending requests are modeled as blocking requirements for the current turn
key UX: When one or more pending requests exist for the current conversation flow, the page enters an awaiting-requests interaction state rather than behaving like ordinary waiting-for-input.
If two pending requests are shown, the user experience treats them as two required items for the current blocked turn; the turn does not resume until both are resolved.

While unresolved pending requests exist, normal composer sending is unavailable, but the existing request cards remain the place where the user completes the required responses, with no new UI introduced in this refactor.
Restart remains allowed while the page is in the awaiting-requests interaction state; once restart begins, it overrides the blocked turn flow and moves the page into restarting.

requirements.name: workspace switching rules are centralized and distinguish switching from saving
key UX: Workspace open, resume, thread switching, and start-new-thread actions are treated as workspace-context switching behavior and follow one shared gate so the page gives consistent allow or block outcomes everywhere.
Workspace switching remains blocked while a turn is running or while unresolved pending requests keep the current turn in the awaiting-requests state.
Saving a workspace as a local favorite is not treated as a workspace-context switch, so it stays allowed even when switching is blocked by the active conversation state.

requirements.name: workspace explorer stays available during active work without enabling unsafe context changes
key UX: The workspace explorer may still be opened while a turn is running or while pending requests are awaiting completion, as long as the current workspace exists.
Opening the explorer does not imply that workspace switching is allowed; the explorer remains scoped to the active workspace context.
Explorer-related actions continue to use the current UI, but their availability and loading states are normalized through the shared page state model.

requirements.name: runtime settings are one immediate-save system including collaboration mode
key UX: All runtime settings, including collaboration mode, follow the same immediate-save behavior when the user changes them; there is no separate temporary apply step inside the settings drawer.
Collaboration mode is treated as a normal member of runtime settings, not as a one-off send-only override path distinct from other runtime preferences.
Current UI controls remain in place, but the underlying state model removes old special-case behavior so runtime changes are stored consistently and reflected through the same preference pipeline.

requirements.name: single-primary-overlay rule
key UX: Only one primary overlay may be open at a time across the workspace sidebar, thread tools sidebar, runtime settings drawer, and workspace explorer.
Opening one primary overlay closes the others through explicit centralized reducer logic instead of a scattered set of imperative boolean handlers.

requirements.name: errors keep one existing display outlet but are typed by source
key UX: This refactor does not add new visual error widgets; user-facing errors continue to flow through the current shared error display outlet.

Behind that unchanged UI, the state model records typed error kinds such as bootstrap, send, interrupt, restart, rollback, compact, review-start, workspace switch, workspace save, thread history, pending request, workspace file open, and workspace file save.
Typed errors allow future UI improvements without redoing the state model, while immediately making state transitions and tests more accurate in the current UI.

requirements.name: operation status is normalized by action family
key UX: Sending, interrupting, restarting, loading thread history, switching workspace context, submitting pending requests, opening workspace files, saving workspace files, rollback, compact, and review start each expose a normalized operation status instead of ad hoc booleans.
The page derives button disabled and busy behavior from those normalized statuses so current controls stay visually familiar while becoming behaviorally consistent.
Operation normalization also makes it possible to distinguish whether the page is blocked by a long-running command, by unresolved requests, or by ordinary session state.

requirements.name: behavior rules are covered by reducer and selector tests instead of only layout-level tests
key UX: Core rules such as send availability, running-turn restrictions, pending-request blocking, restart allowance during running turns, overlay exclusivity, runtime immediate-save behavior, and typed error routing are covered by focused state transition tests.
Existing component-level UI can keep its current shape, but the product behavior becomes safer to refactor because rules are asserted directly in reducers and selectors.
The feature remains aligned with the no-new-ui scope by shifting test coverage toward state behavior instead of relying only on broad rendered page scenarios.
